implementation_notes: Default realization for Kotlin back ends: the same JPA surface as Java - one @Version attribute on the root entity, checked when the root row is updated, surfaced as OptimisticLockException (or an optimistic-lock failure at commit). Kotlin adds nothing special here: entity classes are ordinary classes, and Spring Boot's @Transactional plus a retry wrapper is how conflicts are handled. As in Java, a write path that touches only members does not trigger the check, so member writes must be funnelled through the root.

variants.idiom_name: JPA @Version on the root entity (Hibernate provider)
pitfalls: Kotlin's val/var choice does not affect Hibernate's tracking: both property and field access strategies still rely on the provider detecting a dirty root for the version bump.
@Transactional proxies only intercept external calls; an internal method call inside the same class runs without the transaction that is supposed to scope the version check.

variants.name: one kotlinx.coroutines Mutex per aggregate root
variants.implementation_notes: The in-process realization for coroutine services that own the cluster in memory: keep a ConcurrentHashMap<Long, Mutex> keyed by the cluster id and wrap every edit in mutex.withLock so exactly one coroutine at a time touches root and members. The Mutex replaces the classic lock manager and is non-reentrant by design - a nested lock of the same root suspends forever - and it coordinates only within one process, so the durable side still needs a row lock or version token.
pitfalls: The Mutex suspends rather than blocks, but a withLock around a blocking JDBC call still parks a thread - keep the critical section free of blocking I/O or use a dispatcher that can afford it.
computeIfAbsent plus withLock must not be nested for the same id (Mutex is non-reentrant), and the map's entries need eviction once a cluster is idle.
